teaching.request: A class about fair comparisons gives only these observations: printer A used blue ink on rough paper and its text blurred; printer B used black ink on smooth paper and its text stayed sharp. A student concludes that blue ink causes blurring. Another can repeat 'hold things constant' but cannot design the next comparison. Using just the teaching reference, write the passage the lecturer could teach from here. Show a meaningful controlled comparison, what its outcomes would and would not resolve, how to respond differently to the two student difficulties, and what observable performance would give better evidence of understanding. The sample contains no other data.
teaching.answer:
Which of our two pages tells us how black ink behaves on rough paper in printer A? Neither does. A printed blue on rough paper and the text blurred. B printed black on smooth paper and the text stayed sharp. If you think blue ink caused the blur, you’ve picked out a real difference between the pages. Now try a rival explanation. Suppose *either* ink blurs on rough paper and stays sharp on smooth paper. Would we have seen anything different? We’d have seen exactly these two results. We could tell a similar story about the printers. The first pair of pages gives all three explanations room to stand.

If you know the phrase “hold things constant” and still need to decide what to print, start with the result you wish you had. We’re missing a black-ink partner for A’s blue print. Assuming A can use both inks, write two orders for printer A. In both, use the same text and settings and a sheet from the same pack of rough paper. Specify blue ink in one order and black in the other. Now run both jobs several times, varying which goes first. Choose the same way to judge every sheet. For instance, count how many of the same ten pairs of letters have lost the visible gap between them.

What would those prints tell us? If blue repeatedly closes more gaps, changing between these two inks makes a difference on A with rough paper. That leaves open whether the color itself explains the difference and whether we would see it on smooth paper. If both inks blur to a similar degree, we’ve found little evidence that switching ink helps in this setup. Both printer A and the rough paper were present for every sheet, so that result cannot tell us which of them explains the blur. If black repeatedly closes more gaps, the difference runs against the original prediction. Each outcome is possible. We’ve only seen the two original pages.

Now put away the print orders. Imagine the print shop is deciding whether it would gain anything by replacing printer A with printer B. Write the two jobs you’d ask the shop to run and the result that would justify switching for those jobs. Try this before reading on.

One fair pair would use the same black ink, smooth paper, text and settings on the two printers, provided both can run that job. If B consistently prints those letters more sharply, you have evidence for using B for that work. If your first plan also gave B different paper, circle that change and revise the orders so a difference in sharpness can be traced to the printer. On a later problem, I’d ask you to design the comparison before I name what to hold constant. Your two runnable orders, your reason for pairing them, and the limit you place on your conclusion would show how far you can carry the idea on your own.

law.request: This is a fictitious seminar rule, with no background law assumed. A claim survives if timely notice was received OR a waiver was signed by the proper officer. Both routes require an active membership on the filing date. The board's only evidence of membership is a spreadsheet and two summaries copied from that spreadsheet. A courier log establishes dispatch just before the deadline; the recipient's log is unavailable. An authentic waiver signed by the proper officer is in the packet. A three-member panel agreed only on dismissal in a different case: each judge relied on a different ground, and no voting or precedential rule beyond this description is supplied. Propose an answer a lecturer could give to 'the dispatch proof failed, so we lose, and the old panel proves it.' Map the remaining route, distinguish evidence from authority, and revise your answer first if archival membership is confirmed, then if it is independently disproved. Use only the legal reasoning reference and the stated facts.
law.answer:
Ask first what would happen if the notice had definitely arrived late. Could this claim still survive? **Yes, if the claimant was an active member on the filing date.** The proper officer signed an authentic waiver. The seminar rule gives that act the same capacity as timely receipt to preserve an active member’s claim. The signed document establishes that the act occurred. The rule supplies its legal effect.

Now return to the courier log. It establishes exactly when the notice was sent in relation to the deadline. The first route requires receipt by the deadline. A notice dispatched just before the cutoff could have arrived on either side of it. The missing recipient’s log leaves that question open. We can therefore set the notice route aside for now without treating late delivery as a fact or abandoning the waiver route.

Both routes meet at one factual question. Was membership active **on the filing date**? There are three membership documents, but the two summaries reproduce a single spreadsheet. If its entry were mistaken, all three could agree for precisely that reason. The spreadsheet remains evidence whose date and reliability matter. Its copies add no independent confirmation. With no further basis for assessing the entry and no stipulated burden or standard of proof, the present answer is conditional.

What does the old decision add? All three judges dismissed that other claim. A judge who voted for dismissal on one ground did not thereby endorse either colleague’s ground. To treat the decision as controlling here, we would need an applicable proposition and a rule giving it that force. The account supplies neither a shared rationale nor a rule for combining the opinions. The order settles the disposition of that case and supplies no finding about this claimant’s membership, notice, or waiver.

1. **The archive confirms active membership on the filing date.** The claim survives through the waiver. We can give that answer even while the date of receipt remains unknown.
2. **Independent evidence then establishes that the claimant was inactive on that date.** Taking that disproof as established requires revising the result. The claim fails because both routes require active membership. The officer’s signature remains genuine, and even a newly recovered log showing timely receipt could not cure the missing condition.

repair.request: Our recording is unavailable. Here is the transcript: 'Today's filter uses a pressure censor. Say it again: pressure sensor. The cens... the sensor takes three readings. “The failure rate rose ten percent,” was my wording yesterday: it went from thirty percent to forty percent. I may have used the wrong unit. The signer sounded like Lee or Li. Which spelling goes in the index?' An autogenerated recap from this same transcript spells it Li twice. A printed staff list has both Lee and Li, with no roles. Show a cleaned evidence-preserving reading, account for the consequential editorial decisions, and explain what evidence would settle the name and the numerical distinction. Use only the transcript repair reference. Do not add an assertion about what the recording sounds like.
repair.answer:
## Cleaned reading

> Today’s filter uses a pressure sensor. The sensor takes three readings. “The failure rate rose ten percent” was my wording yesterday. It went from thirty percent to forty percent. I may have used the wrong unit. The signer sounded like Lee or Li. Which spelling goes in the index?

## Editorial decisions

**Pressure sensor.** The transcript supplies the speaker’s own replacement, “Say it again: pressure sensor,” and the next completed phrase repeats “the sensor.” That supports using *sensor* in both sentences and dropping the abandoned “cens...” before its completed counterpart. The number of readings stays at three. The original transcript preserves the sequence if the correction itself matters. (Einsohn and Schwartz, pp. 211–213.)

**The rate.** The quotation marks enclose the speaker’s account of yesterday’s wording. I kept “ten percent” inside them and retained today’s qualification outside them. On the reported figures, subtracting 30% from 40% gives a rise of **10 percentage points**. Measuring that rise against its starting value gives (40 − 30) / 30 = ⅓, a **33⅓% relative increase**. A 10% relative increase from 30% would reach 33%. The endpoints settle both calculations. To establish which comparison yesterday’s statement was intended to report, ask the speaker whether the ten referred to a difference on the percentage scale or a change relative to the starting rate. To check the rates themselves, consult the underlying figures with their period labels and denominators. (Einsohn and Schwartz, pp. 194–196, 208–213, 247–253.)

**The index.** Leave the personal-name entry pending and retain both candidate spellings in the editorial query. The speaker raises both possibilities. The two occurrences of *Li* in the recap descend from that same transcript. The staff list establishes that both spellings occur on staff, but it assigns neither person the role of signer. A copy of the relevant signed document with a legible printed name, or confirmation from the signer identifying the document and spelling their name, would support an entry. (Hill and King, pp. ix–x, xv; Einsohn and Schwartz, pp. 52–54.)
